title: What are learning outcomes?
description: Learning outcomes state what a learner will know and be able to do after learning. Formal definitions, regulator expectations, how to write them, examples.
shortAnswer: A learning outcome is a statement of what a learner is expected to know, understand and be able to do as a result of a course, unit or learning activity. National and regional qualification frameworks define them formally, typically in terms of knowledge, skills and how the learner applies them with autonomy and responsibility. Good outcomes are specific, observable and assessable, and they drive both teaching and assessment design.
keyTakeaways: Learning outcomes describe results for the learner, not topics the teacher will cover.
Qualification frameworks express outcomes in similar dimensions: knowledge, skills, and either their application (the AQF) or responsibility and autonomy (the European Qualifications Framework).

Regulators can make outcomes enforceable: in Australia, for example, higher education providers must specify course learning outcomes and assess all of them before completion under the Higher Education Standards Framework.
An outcome that cannot be assessed is a warning sign: rewrite it with an observable verb and a context.

sections.heading: How do qualification frameworks define learning outcomes?

blocks.text: Qualification frameworks provide the most widely used definitions. The Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) [glossary](https://www.aqf.edu.au/publication/aqf-glossary) defines learning outcomes as "the expression of the set of knowledge, skills and the application of the knowledge and skills a person has acquired and is able to demonstrate as a result of learning." The [AQF Second Edition](https://www.aqf.edu.au/framework/australian-qualifications-framework) uses these three dimensions to define each of its 10 levels and each qualification type.

blocks.caption: The three AQF dimensions of learning outcomes
head: Dimension
What it describes
rows: What a graduate knows and understands, described by depth, breadth, kinds of knowledge and complexity
What a graduate can do, such as cognitive, technical, communication and creative skills
The context in which knowledge and skills are applied, expressed as autonomy, responsibility and accountability

blocks.text: The European Qualifications Framework (EQF) uses a close equivalent. Annex I of the [Council Recommendation of May 22, 2017 on the European Qualifications Framework for lifelong learning](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32017H0615%2801%29) defines learning outcomes as "statements regarding what a learner knows, understands and is able to do on completion of a learning process, which are defined in terms of knowledge, skills and responsibility and autonomy".
How outcomes change between levels is covered in [AQF levels and learning outcomes](/regulations/aqf-levels-and-learning-outcomes).

sections.heading: What do regulators require of learning outcomes?

blocks.text: Some regulators make learning outcomes an enforceable requirement. In Australian higher education, for example, the Higher Education Standards Framework (Threshold Standards) 2021 requires providers to specify expected learning outcomes and to assess them. Standard 1.4.1 of the [Higher Education Standards Framework](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2021L00488/latest/text) requires that expected learning outcomes for each course are "specified, consistent with the level and field of education of the qualification awarded, and informed by national and international comparators."

Standard 1.4.2 requires outcomes to cover discipline specific and generic outcomes, including knowledge and skills for employment and further study and skills in independent and critical thinking. Standard 1.4.4 requires that students demonstrate all specified outcomes on completion, whether assessed at unit level, course level or both. The Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA) explains how it tests these in its [course design guidance note](https://www.teqsa.gov.au/guides-resources/resources/guidance-notes/guidance-note-course-design-including-learning-outcomes-and-assessment); see also [TEQSA HESF course design requirements](/regulations/teqsa-hesf-course-design-requirements).

In the vocational education and training (VET) sector, the equivalent of learning outcomes is expressed through units of competency, which state workplace performance rather than learning outcomes in the academic sense.

sections.heading: How are learning outcomes different from learning objectives and competencies?

blocks.text: Learning outcomes describe what the learner will be able to do; learning objectives are often written from the teacher's side, describing what the course aims to cover. Many organizations use the terms interchangeably, but writing from the learner's side makes outcomes easier to assess.

items: A **competency** in a [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework) describes performance in a role; a learning outcome describes the result of a specific learning experience that contributes to it.
[Constructive alignment](/glossary/constructive-alignment) is the design principle that aligns teaching and assessment to the outcomes.
[Curriculum mapping](/glossary/curriculum-mapping) shows where each outcome is taught, practiced and assessed across a program.

sections.heading: What does a well written learning outcome look like?

blocks.text: The examples below are illustrative, taken from a privacy training program for customer service staff.

head: Weak outcome
Problem
Stronger outcome
rows: Identify personal information in a customer record and explain which handling rule applies
Recognize a suspected data breach in a scenario and report it through the correct channel within the required timeframe
Apply the privacy policy to decide whether a caller may be given account information

blocks.text: More on writing them is in [how to write measurable learning outcomes](/guides/how-to-write-measurable-learning-outcomes).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry writes learning outcomes as part of the framework, each linked to the obligation or procedure it serves and to at least one assessment point. Content is written to those outcomes, not the other way around.

faqs.q: What verbs should learning outcomes use?
faqs.a: Use observable verbs that match the level of performance expected, such as identify, explain, apply, compare, design or evaluate. Avoid verbs that cannot be observed directly, such as understand, know or appreciate. Taxonomies such as Bloom's taxonomy are commonly used to choose verbs at the right level.

faqs.q: How many learning outcomes should a course have?
faqs.a: Enough to describe the important results and few enough that each is taught and assessed properly. Short workplace modules often need only a handful. If outcomes cannot all be assessed in the time available, the list is too long or the outcomes are too granular.

faqs.q: Do compliance training courses need learning outcomes?
faqs.a: Yes. Without outcomes, a compliance course can only show attendance. Outcomes linked to specific obligations make it possible to assess whether staff can apply the rule, and to show a regulator or auditor what the training was designed to achieve.

faqs.q: Are learning outcomes the same across VET and higher education?
faqs.a: In Australia, for example, both sectors sit within the AQF, which describes qualifications through learning outcomes. In practice, VET expresses requirements as units of competency with performance and knowledge evidence, while higher education providers write their own course and unit learning outcomes under the Higher Education Standards Framework.

factCheck.claim: AQF glossary definition of learning outcomes
AQF has 10 levels; levels and qualification types defined by learning outcomes in three dimensions: knowledge, skills, application of knowledge and skills (autonomy, responsibility, accountability)
HESF Standards 1.4.1, 1.4.2 and 1.4.4 text on specifying, scope of and demonstrating learning outcomes
TEQSA guidance note on course design covers learning outcomes (Section 1.4) and course design (Section 3.1)

EQF Council Recommendation 2017/C 189/03, Annex I(e): learning outcomes means statements regarding what a learner knows, understands and is able to do on completion of a learning process, defined in terms of knowledge, skills and responsibility and autonomy.
